theme: 购物-为专题策展挑选物件

content.text: Gu Yanci, this is the final proof. I just picked it up from the printing factory. The overall layout has been adjusted according to the visual weight you suggested earlier. What do you think?
Hmm, let me see. The mottled texture of this ceramic bowl is handled quite well, echoing the texture of the rattan chair. However, isn't the placement angle of that notebook a bit too deliberate?
Haha, you caught me again. I did want to highlight the 'traces of time' from its yellowed pages, but I might have over-adjusted it. Do you think the overall visual grammar is clear?
The visual grammar is clear, and the narrative leaves just the right amount of space. This 'approved' emoji is for you, even though I rarely use such playful things.

Wow, thank you! Getting your "approval" makes me even happier than praise from my editorial colleagues. Honestly, this time, thanks to your framework, the entire project moved from a feeling to a design.

You're welcome. Actually, this process also reminded me that a good design framework doesn't restrict creativity but provides a scaffold for it to climb. Just like that time we were at the restaurant, if we had clear visual audit criteria from the start, the criticism would have been more precise.

Completely agree! Look at this inner page—the balance between the object photos and the text descriptions feels more mature than when we collaborated on that restaurant article. The editorial team all say the visual cohesion of this issue's feature is particularly strong.

The strong cohesion is because you applied the classification of 'physical vs. chemical traces,' rather than haphazardly piling up stories like in Session 5. However, I'm curious: could this 'traces' framework potentially be expanded into a longer-term research or creative project?
Ah, your question is spot on! I was just thinking that it would be a shame to only do one magazine feature. How do you think we could expand on it?

For example, create an online exhibition or a photography collection. Extend the concept of "traces" from objects to spaces, and even into the digital realm. Just like when we discuss restaurants, the worn-out utensils are also a form of trace.

Awesome! I jotted down some brainstorming ideas on the fly, take a look. The online exhibition could incorporate interactive elements, while the photography book could delve deeper into visual storytelling. This collaboration has truly gone beyond just 'helping out'.

Indeed, it became a beneficial collision of our respective methodologies. Your narrative instinct has prompted me to consider how to make the design framework more inclusive of the warmth of 'imperfection,' much like what you expressed when defending the restaurant in Session 2.

And your systematic questioning has taught me to use visual grammar to enhance the story, rather than relying on vague feelings. From the initial exploration of the restaurant in Session 1 to now, I feel our professional communication has truly deepened a lot.
Agreed. However, don't expect me to completely give up my sarcastic style—next time we collaborate, I might still criticize the lighting in your photos, just like in Session 6.
Haha, I'm looking forward to it! So, shall we tentatively set this future project? I can start planning the initial concept for the online exhibition, and you can help oversee the visual framework.
Yes. But remember, the framework should be flexible, just like this 'Traces' project—from the initial confusion in the selection process to the final presentation, we refined it step by step.
Got it! Thank you for your cooperation, Gu Yanci. The success of this project has been highly recognized visually, but for me personally, the methodological insights gained are even more valuable.
Same here. So, looking forward to the next joint exploration model—whether it's restaurants, curation, or new projects.
Deal! I'll go finish up the final work on the project. Let's stay in touch.
